title: Java Foundations, Data Types & Scanner
subtitle: Understand how Java runs, where values live, and how to read input clearly.
goals: Explain source → bytecode → JVM
Read the structure of a Java program
Distinguish primitive values from reference values
Relate local variables and objects to stack and heap
Read, validate and consume input with Scanner

sections.title: JDK, JRE and JVM
paragraphs: The Java Development Kit, or JDK, is the toolkit used to develop Java software. It includes javac for compilation, java for launching programs, debugging and documentation tools, and the runtime components required by those tools.

The Java Runtime Environment, or JRE, provides what a Java program needs to run: the JVM, standard libraries and supporting runtime components. The JDK includes these runtime components as well as development tools such as javac; a runtime alone does not provide that compiler.

The Java Virtual Machine, or JVM, is the abstract execution environment for class files. The standard library is the collection of reusable APIs—such as String, Scanner, List, Files, and Thread—that applications call instead of rebuilding common facilities.
sections.note: Select a JDK for the project, not merely an editor. Without a configured JDK, the IDE has no compiler or Java platform against which to check the program.

sections.title: Skeleton of a Java Program
paragraphs: A .java source file can contain more than one class, as well as package and import declarations outside the classes. For this first program, use one public class named First and save it as First.java. Java also has other type declarations, such as interfaces; not every source file must declare a class.
sections.note: Names must match exactly: First and first are different names. Because the declaration is public class First, save the file as First.java. String and System are standard Java types in java.lang, which is available automatically; Scanner belongs to java.util, so it needs import java.util.Scanner.
sections.html:
Read the main method, one piece at a time

public
Access modifier: the method is accessible from outside the class.
static
No First object is needed to invoke this method.
void
Return type: this method returns no value.
main
The method name recognized by the launcher for this entry-point form.
String[] args
Parameter: an array of command-line strings. args is the chosen variable name.
What does String[] args mean?

args is a list (an array) of text values supplied when you launch the program. In the terminal command below, First is the class to run; the words after it become the arguments.

java First Candice 2026

args[0] is "Candice" and args[1] is "2026". Array positions start at 0, and even 2026 arrives as text.

The Hello World program above never uses args, so those extra words do not change its output. A statement such as System.out.println(args[0]); would print Candice for this command.
sections.lead: In the Java 21 programs in this course, methods and executable statements belong inside a class; statements such as printing or reading input go inside a method.

sections.title: Java data types: Primitive and Reference
paragraphs: Java variables come in two kinds. A primitive variable holds the value itself: after int x = 10;, x stores 10. A reference variable holds a reference to an object: after String s = new String("hi");, s holds a reference to that String object — or it could hold null, meaning "no object." Think of a reference as a way to locate an object on the heap, rather than an address you can inspect or manipulate in Java.

Assigning a primitive copies the value, while assigning a reference copies the reference. Two references to the same mutable object see changes made to that object through either reference. String objects are immutable, so use the array example in the next part to see shared changes.
emphasis: A primitive variable holds the value itself
A reference variable holds a reference to an object
String objects are immutable, so use the array example in the next part to see shared changes.

sections.title: Java memory: Method Area, Stack and Heap
paragraphs: For a local declaration such as Student s = new Student(), s holds a reference in the current method’s stack frame; the new Student object belongs to the heap. The method area holds class information and method code.

sections.title: Scanner: sources, keyboard input, validation and consumption

subsections.title: A reference type and its input sources
paragraphs: Scanner is a class, so Scanner is a reference type. In Scanner input = new Scanner(System.in), input holds a reference to a Scanner object; it does not hold the text or an integer. The object reads text from a source and its methods return values such as int, double, boolean or String.

Choose the source when constructing the Scanner. Choose what to read when calling a method. A token is one piece of text separated by a delimiter; Scanner uses whitespace by default. For example, "10 20" contains two tokens. The same nextInt() method can read an integer from keyboard input, a file or an existing string.
subsections.note: The source provides text. nextInt() converts a token to int; next() returns token text; nextLine() returns line text. The Scanner itself remains an object.

subsections.title: Read keyboard input
paragraphs: Import java.util.Scanner, create one Scanner connected to System.in, and call a reading method for each value you expect. A keyboard read can wait until input is available. These first examples assume that the user enters the requested types.
Spaces separate tokens and Enter ends a line; neither signals the end of input, so a keyboard loop using hasNext() may wait for more input.

Token methods skip leading whitespace, so numbers may be separated by spaces or line breaks. next() reads one token; nextLine() reads the rest of a line, including spaces within it. Decimal examples below use Locale.ROOT so a decimal point is interpreted consistently.
subsections.note: Use one shared keyboard Scanner. Closing it also closes System.in. A file Scanner owns a separate resource and should be closed.

subsections.title: Validate before reading
paragraphs: Validation means checking before you read. hasNextInt() asks: “Can the next token be read as an int?” It returns true or false, but leaves the token where it is.

If the answer is true, use nextInt() to read the integer. If it is false, show a message instead. For example, 20 is an int; hello and 3.5 are not. Calling nextInt() on hello without checking would cause InputMismatchException.

visuals.title: A validation loop must always move forward

items.label: Invalid branch
items.detail: Consume the bad token with next()

items.label: Repeat or finish
items.detail: Never inspect the same bad token forever

subsections.title: Consume input and understand the nextLine() trap
emphasis: Consume simply means read and move past input.
paragraphs: Consume simply means read and move past input. hasNextInt() only checks; nextInt() reads an integer; next() reads one token as text.

For hello 20, next() can read past hello so nextInt() can reach 20. The word hello is invalid as an int, but next() can still read it as a String. Repeating a check without reading would keep checking the same hello.

visuals.title: From source file to running program
visuals.description: Compilation and execution are separate stages. The compiler produces bytecode; the JVM executes it.

items.detail: Uses the local OS and hardware

title: Method Overloading & Object-Oriented Programming
subtitle: Choose a method by its parameters, then design objects with state and useful operations.
goals: Write overloaded methods with different parameter lists
Explain abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism
Turn properties and operations into fields and methods
Control access with getters and setters
Initialize objects with overloaded constructors
Create and use an array of object references

sections.title: Method Overloading
paragraphs: Overloading lets several methods share one name when their parameter lists are different. Start with what a method receives and what it returns, then compare the calls.

subsections.title: One name, different parameter lists
paragraphs: In int max(int x, int y), int before max is the return type; x and y are parameters. In max(10, 15), 10 and 15 are arguments. return sends the result back to the caller.
Overloaded methods have the same name but different parameter types, numbers of parameters, or orders of types. Changing only a parameter name or the return type does not create a new overload.
For these ordinary calls, the compiler chooses an overload from the declared argument types. The helpers below are static so main can call them without first creating an object.

visuals.title: Which max method is selected?

subsections.title: Overloading with different parameter types and counts
paragraphs: Use one method name for one idea. area can take a radius or a length and breadth. reverse can receive one integer or an int array. validate can receive a name or an age.
The parameter list must tell the methods apart. area(double length, double breadth) and area(double base, double height) would have the same signature; changing the words does not distinguish them.

sections.title: Object-Oriented Programming
paragraphs: Object-oriented programming organizes a program around objects, combining state (fields) with behavior (methods). Start with the four principles—abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism—then explore classes, constructors and objects through code.

subsections.title: The four OOP principles
paragraphs: Abstraction exposes the useful operations without making the caller manage the internal steps. A television offers turnOn(); its user does not need to operate the circuitry.
Encapsulation keeps related data and methods together and controls access to the data. A private volume field can be changed through a method that checks the allowed range.
Inheritance lets a more specific class build on a more general class. Television extends Device means a television is a kind of device.
Polymorphism lets the same operation use different implementations. A Device reference can call turnOn(), and a Television object can supply the television-specific behavior.

Overloading is often called compile-time polymorphism. Overriding uses the actual object at runtime. Keep these two selection rules separate; later lessons develop overriding and inheritance in detail.

subsections.title: Class, object and reference
paragraphs: A class defines a type. An object is an instance of that class. A reference variable identifies an object: in Circle first = new Circle(), Circle is the type, first is the variable, and new Circle() creates an object.
To design a class, ask: what does it store, and what can it do? A Circle stores radius and calculates area and perimeter. Fields describe state; methods describe behavior.

Each object has its own instance fields. An instance method such as first.area() uses the radius of first’s object. The first examples use public fields so you can see this relationship; data hiding follows.
Choose fields first, then methods that use those fields. A method calculating a result should normally return it; main can decide how to display it.
Use double for dimensions and int for whole-number marks. Use boolean for a yes/no question such as isSquare(). A Student grade can return a char such as A or B.

visuals.title: From properties to operations

subsections.title: Constructors and constructor overloading
paragraphs: A constructor runs when an object is created. It has the class name and no return type, not even void. new Rectangle(4, 3) creates an object and invokes the matching constructor.
A no-argument constructor receives no values; a parameterized constructor receives values. Constructors can be overloaded using different parameter lists, just like methods.

Java supplies a default no-argument constructor only when a class declares no constructor. If you write Rectangle(double length, double breadth), new Rectangle() needs an explicitly declared no-argument constructor.

In this.length = length, this.length is the current object’s field and length is the parameter. this(...) calls another constructor in the same class; in Java 21 it must be the first constructor statement.

subsections.title: Data hiding and encapsulation
paragraphs: With public fields, a caller could assign a negative length. Make the fields private, then provide methods that decide which values may be stored. This is data hiding as part of encapsulation.
A getter returns a value. A setter receives a value and updates the field. In this example, a negative dimension becomes zero, so callers cannot leave a negative value inside the rectangle.

subsections.title: Properties: read-write, read-only and write-only
paragraphs: A property describes the access a class offers to a value. A private field does not automatically need both a getter and a setter. Provide only the operations callers should have.
Read-write means getter plus setter. Read-only means a getter without a public setter. Write-only means a setter without a public getter; internal methods may still use the value.

visuals.title: Choose access deliberately

subsections.title: Arrays of objects
paragraphs: new Subject[2] creates one array with two null reference slots. It does not create two Subject objects. Create each Subject separately and assign its reference into a slot before calling its methods.
A Student can hold that Subject array as a field. This is a has-a relationship: a student has subjects; it does not extend Subject.

The example finishes the design with a constructor, getters and setters. setSubjects(Subject... subjects) uses varargs: the caller can supply several Subject references, which the method receives as an array.

title: Inheritance, Overriding, Polymorphism & Abstract Classes
subtitle: Build a subclass, change its behavior, and use different objects through one common type.
goals: Use extends to create a subclass
Override an inherited instance method
Explain why a parent reference can run child behavior
Define an abstract class and implement its abstract methods

sections.title: Inheritance
paragraphs: Inheritance lets a class build on another class. Animal is the parent class (superclass); Dog is the child class (subclass). class Dog extends Animal expresses an is-a relationship: a Dog is an Animal.
A child can use inherited methods and add its own methods. Here, Dog inherits eat() and adds bark(). We have not changed the parent’s behavior yet.

sections.title: Method overriding
paragraphs: Overriding gives an inherited instance method a new implementation in the child class. In this example, both classes define public void speak(), but Dog supplies its own body.

Use @Override above the child method so the compiler checks that it really overrides a parent method. Keep the same name and parameter types; the examples also keep the same return type and public access.
Overloading was covered in Lesson 2. The table below is the one comparison to remember before moving on.

sections.title: Polymorphism
paragraphs: A parent-type variable can refer to a child object. In Animal pet = new Dog(), Animal is the variable’s declared type, while Dog is the actual object’s type. No extra Animal object is created.

The declared type determines which methods you may call through the variable. The actual object determines which overridden instance-method body runs. Therefore pet.speak() runs Dog.speak(). This runtime choice is called dynamic method dispatch.
The useful result: one loop can call speak() on different Animal objects. Each object supplies its own behavior, so the loop needs no separate test for Dog or Cat.

sections.title: Abstract classes and abstract methods
paragraphs: An abstract class is a base class that cannot be instantiated directly. An abstract method declares an operation without a body. A concrete child class must implement the abstract methods it inherits.
Every shape should have an area, but there is no single formula for all shapes. Shape declares area(); Rectangle and Circle provide their own formulas.

An abstract class can also contain fields, constructors and ordinary methods with bodies. Here describe() is shared, while its call to area() uses the actual shape’s implementation. You can write Shape s = new Circle(2), but not new Shape().
sections.html:
Optional reference: additional inheritance rules
  • super.method() calls the inherited parent implementation. super(...) calls a parent constructor; constructors are not inherited or overridden.
  • A final method cannot be overridden. A private parent method is not inherited as an overridable method.
  • Static methods are hidden, not dynamically overridden. Field access also depends on the declared reference type.
  • An override cannot reduce accessibility. A reference return type may be more specific, and checked exceptions cannot be broadened beyond the parent declaration.
  • Assigning a child object to a parent reference is upcasting. Downcasting requires a compatible actual object or it fails at runtime; use polymorphic methods when possible.

rows: Offer different parameter lists under one name
Provide child behavior for an inherited method

title: Interfaces & Nested Classes
subtitle: Express capabilities independently of inheritance and place helper types in the right scope.
goals: Implement interface contracts
Explain callback control flow
Distinguish four nested-class forms
Understand outer-instance access and local capture

sections.title: An interface describes a capability
paragraphs: An interface declares a contract that different classes can implement. A class extends at most one class but may implement several interfaces. A variable of an interface type can refer to any object implementing it, allowing the caller to depend on the capability rather than the implementation.

Ordinary interface abstract methods are public, so their class implementations must be public. Interface fields are public static final constants, not per-object state. Interfaces may also have default and static methods; private helper methods support interface implementations. A default method provides behavior, but does not give the interface ordinary instance fields.

sections.title: Abstract class or interface?
paragraphs: Use an abstract class when related types share state, construction rules and partial implementation. Use an interface to express a role that otherwise unrelated classes can adopt. A class can combine both: extend a shared base and implement several capabilities.

If unrelated interfaces provide conflicting defaults with the same signature, the implementing class must resolve the conflict explicitly. Java’s multiple interface inheritance does not mean that it inherits multiple independent parent-class object states.

sections.title: Callbacks reverse who chooses the behavior
paragraphs: A callback is an operation supplied to another component so that the component can invoke it at the appropriate time. A Button can know how to signal a click without knowing whether the application will save, print or navigate. The caller provides the action through an interface.

The callback is still an ordinary method invocation. The useful distinction is responsibility: the component decides when to call; the supplied object decides what happens. Anonymous classes provide a compact implementation before Lambda syntax is introduced.

sections.title: Member inner classes carry an outer object
paragraphs: A non-static member inner class is associated with one enclosing instance. It can directly access private instance fields of that outer object. Construction therefore requires an outer instance first.

sections.title: Static nested classes do not capture an instance
paragraphs: A static nested class is namespaced inside its enclosing class but has no implicit outer object. It can directly use only static members unless a reference to an outer object is passed explicitly. Choose this form when nesting improves organization but instance capture is unnecessary.

sections.title: Local and anonymous classes
paragraphs: A local class is declared inside a block, usually a method, and is visible only there. An anonymous class defines and instantiates a one-off subclass or interface implementation in one expression. Both may capture local variables only when those variables are final or effectively final.

Anonymous classes remain useful when a one-off implementation needs fields, several methods, or special initialization. When a functional interface needs only a short behavior, a lambda is usually clearer.

sections.title: Choosing the smallest honest scope
paragraphs: Nesting is useful when a type serves only its enclosing abstraction. It reduces namespace clutter and can hide implementation details. Excessive nesting, however, makes construction and testing harder. Promote a nested type to a top-level class when it develops an independent responsibility or is reused elsewhere.

title: Packages, Access & Exception Foundations
subtitle: Organize types into boundaries and distinguish a failure from its handling policy.
goals: Match package names to project layout
Apply access modifiers across files
Classify Java failures and exception types
Trace try/catch and exception propagation

sections.title: Project structure and packages
paragraphs: A package name is a qualified type namespace, while a source root is the directory above the package hierarchy. A class declared in package ca.school.app conventionally lives at ca/school/app beneath the source root. Compilation output mirrors that hierarchy beneath the output directory.

Keeping generated .class files outside src prevents source and build artifacts from being mixed. Share source files and project configuration when needed; do not treat out or bin directories as the authoritative program.

sections.title: Packages and access boundaries
paragraphs: Packages create namespaces and establish an access boundary. public is visible everywhere; protected is visible in the package and to subclasses under Java's inheritance rules; package-private is visible only within the package; private is visible only within the declaring top-level class and its nested types.

Package names conventionally use a reversed domain, such as ca.school.registration. The package declaration, directory structure, imports, compiler output, and classpath must agree. Packages are therefore part of a program's architecture, not merely labels at the top of files.

sections.title: A package is tested across files
paragraphs: Package access cannot be understood from a single isolated class. A useful exercise places a public model class and a package-private factory in ca.school.model, then places Main in ca.school.app. Main may import and use the public model class, but it cannot import the package-private factory.

Compile the complete source tree into a separate output directory. If the package statement and directory hierarchy disagree, the compiler or launcher will report that the expected type cannot be found.

sections.title: Access is checked at the declaration boundary
paragraphs: public members are accessible wherever their enclosing type is accessible. A member with no modifier is package-private and is available within its package. private members are restricted to their enclosing top-level class’s nest of nested types. protected permits package access and controlled access from subclasses outside the package.

Across packages, protected instance access from a subclass is not a general permission to inspect any arbitrary parent object. The qualifying reference must satisfy the subclass access rule. Importing a type only shortens its name; it never bypasses access checks. Top-level classes can be public or package-private, not private or protected.

sections.title: Compile-time, logical, and runtime failures
paragraphs: A compile-time error prevents class files from being produced; examples include malformed syntax, an unknown name, or an incompatible type. A logical error compiles and runs but produces the wrong result because the algorithm or formula is incorrect. A runtime failure occurs while the program is executing; many, but not all, runtime failures are represented by exceptions.

Exception handling addresses exceptional runtime control flow. It cannot repair invalid syntax, and it does not automatically detect an incorrect algorithm. Those problems require compiler feedback, tests, tracing, and debugging.
sections.note: Classify the failure before choosing a remedy: compiler diagnostics, tests and debugging, or exception handling.

sections.title: The exception hierarchy
paragraphs: Throwable has two major branches. Error represents serious JVM or environment failures that applications normally do not recover from. Exception represents conditions application code may handle. Checked exceptions must be caught or declared; RuntimeException and its subclasses are unchecked.

Checked versus unchecked is a compiler rule, not a measure of severity. A checked exception is appropriate when callers can reasonably anticipate and recover from the condition. An unchecked exception commonly reports a violated precondition, invalid state, or programming mistake.
sections.note: Choose an exception type according to the API contract and the caller's recovery options, not simply according to how alarming the failure feels.

sections.title: try, catch, and propagation
paragraphs: A try block contains operations that share a recovery policy. Several catch blocks may follow one try block and are tested from most specific to most general. A nested try statement is legal when an inner operation has a genuinely different recovery boundary, although excessive nesting usually obscures the control flow. If no compatible catch exists, the exception propagates to the caller and the current method ends.
A catch block should add useful context, recover, or translate the exception. Catching Exception and doing nothing destroys evidence and allows the program to continue in an unknown state.

sections.title: Read a stack trace from the failure outward
paragraphs: An exception stack trace identifies the exception type and message, followed by call frames. Find the first frame in your own code and inspect the operation at that line. The caller frames show how execution arrived there. A cause chain may explain an underlying file or parsing failure.

A catch block runs only for a compatible exception. Once a throw occurs, the remaining statements in that try path are skipped. If the method cannot handle the failure, propagation unwinds the call stack until a handler is found; otherwise the thread ends with an uncaught exception.

sections.title: Specific recovery belongs before general recovery
paragraphs: Order catch blocks from more specific types to broader types. A broad catch placed first may make a later specific catch unreachable. Multi-catch combines unrelated exception alternatives when the recovery policy is identical. A nested try is useful only when an inner operation has a distinct recovery policy.

Do not confuse guarding expected user input with catching every failure. hasNextInt() can avoid an ordinary invalid-token exception; catching a domain exception can report a rule violation. Neither technique justifies hiding all exceptions or continuing with incomplete state.

title: Exceptions, Resources & First Threads
subtitle: Make failure contracts explicit, close owned resources, and start concurrent work.
goals: Distinguish throw from throws
Create and handle a checked domain exception
Read files with Scanner and automatic cleanup
Compare Thread.start() with an ordinary run() call

sections.title: throw and throws
paragraphs: throw is an executable statement that transfers control by raising one exception object. throws is part of a method declaration and announces checked exceptions that may escape. A custom exception gives a domain failure a precise name and can carry a cause or additional context.

sections.title: Cleanup and try-with-resources
paragraphs: finally executes after try and catch whether the operation succeeds or fails, apart from abnormal process termination. It is suitable for cleanup but should not return or throw a new unrelated exception that hides the original failure.

For AutoCloseable objects, try-with-resources is safer. Resources declared in the header close automatically in reverse order. If both the body and close operation fail, the close failure is retained as a suppressed exception rather than replacing the primary one.

sections.title: Custom exceptions give a failure a domain name
paragraphs: A custom checked exception extends Exception. Its constructor normally passes a meaningful message to super; a second constructor can preserve an underlying cause. A method declaring throws InvalidScoreException requires its caller to catch or declare that checked failure.

An exception object carries evidence, not a repair strategy. The method that detects the invalid value may be unable to ask a user for another value. The caller at the interaction boundary can decide whether to reject the record, retry or stop.

sections.title: finally observes both success and failure
paragraphs: A finally block executes as control leaves its try/catch, including an ordinary return. It is not an absolute guarantee against JVM termination or a process crash. Returning or throwing an unrelated exception from finally can replace an earlier result or failure and should be avoided.

Use finally when a cleanup action is not represented by an AutoCloseable resource. For files and streams, prefer try-with-resources: it closes resources in reverse declaration order and preserves close failures as suppressed exceptions when the body has already failed.

sections.title: Files and resource ownership
paragraphs: Scanner applies the same token model to files. A file-backed scanner owns an operating-system resource and belongs in try-with-resources.
Standard input is shared by the process. Closing a scanner wrapping System.in also closes System.in, so the application should decide which component owns that scanner.

sections.title: File input combines token rules with ownership
paragraphs: A file-backed Scanner uses the same token and line operations as keyboard input. Choose whether each record is a token, a full line or several fields. hasNextInt() alone stops at the first non-integer token, so a robust importer must deliberately reject or skip malformed content rather than silently treating it as end of file.

The file path is resolved from the process working directory unless an absolute path is supplied. try-with-resources owns and closes the file scanner. That ownership differs from a shared Scanner around System.in. Error messages should identify the input record or path without discarding the original cause.

sections.title: Multiprogramming, multitasking, and multithreading
paragraphs: Multiprogramming keeps several programs available so that the processor can switch when one cannot continue. Multitasking describes the broader experience of multiple tasks making progress through scheduling. Multithreading applies concurrent execution paths within one process.

A process has its own resource boundary. Threads in that process share objects and class state but have separate call stacks. This distinction explains both the efficiency of communication through shared objects and the need to coordinate access to mutable state.

sections.title: A task describes work; a thread executes it
paragraphs: A Runnable supplies a run() method describing work. A Thread manages an execution path. Extending Thread also works, but implementing Runnable keeps the task reusable and avoids consuming the class’s single superclass slot. The next lesson will coordinate several threads safely.

Calling start() schedules a new thread that will invoke run(). Calling run() directly is an ordinary method call on the current thread. A Thread instance can be started only once. Output order between independent threads is not a dependable indication of program correctness.

title: Thread Lifecycle, Synchronization & Coordination
subtitle: Make shared-state rules explicit and use one monitor to enforce them.
goals: Explain thread states and completion
Handle interruption cooperatively
Protect an entire shared invariant
Use condition loops for wait/notifyAll

sections.title: Lifecycle and scheduling
paragraphs: A Thread begins in NEW, becomes RUNNABLE after start(), may enter BLOCKED, WAITING, or TIMED_WAITING, and ends in TERMINATED. RUNNABLE includes both ready-to-run and currently-running states from the JVM's perspective.

Scheduling order is not guaranteed. Priority and yield are hints, not correctness mechanisms. sleep pauses the current thread until the requested duration elapses unless it is interrupted; scheduling may delay the actual resumption. The method does not release intrinsic locks already held.
sections.note: If a program is correct only when one thread happens to run first, the program is not correctly synchronized.

sections.title: Completion, interruption, and daemon threads
paragraphs: join() waits for another thread to terminate and establishes visibility of its completed work. Interruption is a cooperative cancellation request. Blocking methods often respond by throwing InterruptedException; code should stop, propagate the exception, or restore the interrupted status rather than silently swallowing it.

A daemon thread does not keep the JVM alive after all user threads finish. Set daemon status before start(). Daemons are suitable for background assistance, not for work whose final write or cleanup must be guaranteed.

sections.title: Start workers together; wait for all results
paragraphs: A group of workers can be stored in a Thread array before collections have been introduced. Start every worker in one loop, then join every worker in a second loop. Joining immediately after each start would serialize those tasks and prevent the intended overlap.

A ThreadGroup can associate named platform threads for organizational purposes, but it does not make shared data safe or replace explicit completion. Priority and yield are scheduling hints, not ordering rules. Never use a guessed sleep duration as proof that another task has completed.

sections.title: Race conditions and critical sections
paragraphs: An operation such as value++ is a read-modify-write sequence rather than one indivisible action. Two threads can read the same old value and lose one update.
The critical section is the complete region that reads or changes a shared invariant. Protecting only one statement is insufficient when the rule spans a check followed by an update.

sections.title: One monitor must protect one protocol
paragraphs: synchronized acquires an object's intrinsic monitor. Only code using the same monitor participates in the same mutual-exclusion rule. Locking different objects does not protect shared state.

An ATM check-and-withdraw sequence is one transaction. If checking and withdrawal are synchronized separately, another customer may enter between them. The monitor must cover the complete transaction.
sections.note: State the invariant in one sentence, then verify that every read and write participating in it uses the same lock.

sections.title: wait, notify, and condition loops
paragraphs: wait() releases the current object's monitor and suspends the thread. notify() wakes one waiter; notifyAll() wakes all waiters competing for that monitor. These methods must be called while owning the same monitor.
A waiter tests its condition in a while loop because it may wake spuriously or another thread may consume the condition before the waiter reacquires the monitor.

sections.title: Producer-consumer communication
paragraphs: A producer waits while the shared slot is full, publishes one value, changes the condition, and signals waiters. A consumer waits while the slot is empty, reads the value, changes the condition, and signals again.
Both methods synchronize on the same shared object. Finite production counts and joins make the demonstration repeatable and prevent worker threads from running forever.
sections.note: Despite the older name inter-process communication in some examples, shared-object wait/notify here coordinates threads inside one process.

sections.title: One-to-many coordination
paragraphs: A teacher-and-students example has one writer and several readers. The writer cannot replace the current note until every registered reader has consumed it. Each reader decrements the remaining-reader count and the final reader signals the writer.
The number of readers must be established safely before publication begins. A condition loop protects both early arrival and later wake-up.
sections.note: notifyAll is appropriate when several distinct waiters may need to re-check their own conditions.

sections.title: Keep critical sections deliberate
paragraphs: Holding a monitor during sleep or slow input/output prevents other threads using that monitor from progressing. A short delay may make classroom serialization visible, but production critical sections should contain only the work needed to preserve the invariant.

Higher-level tools such as BlockingQueue, locks, latches, and executors often express common protocols more safely. Understanding monitors remains essential because those tools solve the same coordination problems at a stronger abstraction level.

sections.title: Interrupt is a request, not a forced kill
paragraphs: A thread blocked in sleep(), join() or wait() may receive InterruptedException. It should stop, propagate the exception, or restore the interrupted status if it cannot complete the cancellation decision itself. An empty catch loses the cancellation request.

When a loop does CPU work rather than calling interruptible blocking methods, it can periodically inspect the interrupted status. Do not rely on daemon threads to finish important writes: the JVM may terminate once no non-daemon threads remain.

title: Reflection, Annotations & Lambda Expressions
subtitle: Inspect runtime type information, attach metadata, and pass behavior through an interface.
goals: Inspect and invoke a known public method
Read runtime annotations
Give a lambda a functional-interface target
Use capture and method-reference forms

sections.title: Class objects are runtime type descriptions
paragraphs: Every loaded type has a Class object. It can be obtained with MyType.class, object.getClass(), or Class.forName(). Class<?> means a class object for some unknown type; Class<T> preserves the relationship to a known T.

getDeclaredFields() and getDeclaredMethods() return members declared directly by the class, regardless of visibility. getMethods() returns public methods including inherited methods. Code must not depend on the order of these returned arrays.

sections.title: Built-in annotations communicate intent
paragraphs: @Override asks the compiler to verify that a method actually overrides or implements an inherited declaration. @Deprecated marks an API that callers should avoid and may provide migration guidance. @SuppressWarnings narrows a deliberate compiler-warning suppression to a selected declaration.

@FunctionalInterface verifies that an interface remains a valid lambda target. @SafeVarargs may suppress specific heap-pollution warnings only on eligible final, static, private, or constructor declarations whose variable-argument handling is genuinely safe. These annotations are checked or interpreted by tools; they do not replace the language rules they describe.
sections.note: Use the narrowest annotation scope and do not suppress a warning until its cause is understood.

sections.title: Annotations are metadata, not behavior
paragraphs: An annotation type is declared with @interface. Its elements look like parameterless methods and may have default values. Applying an annotation records metadata; nothing happens unless the compiler, a tool, or runtime code reads and acts on it.
@Target limits where the annotation may appear. @Retention chooses whether it exists only in source, in the class file, or at runtime. Reflection can read only annotations retained at runtime.

sections.title: Discovering and invoking marked methods
paragraphs: A framework-like program can scan methods, request a particular annotation, validate its values, and invoke the method. Reflective invocation wraps a failure thrown by the target method, so production code must unwrap and report the underlying cause carefully.

sections.title: Trade-offs and boundaries
paragraphs: Reflection reduces direct coupling and supports extensible tools, but names and signatures may fail only at runtime. Private-access overrides weaken encapsulation and may be restricted by Java modules. Reflective code is also harder to navigate and test.

Prefer normal interfaces, constructors, and method calls for application logic. Use reflection at infrastructure boundaries where dynamic discovery provides clear value, then validate early and convert failures into meaningful domain errors.

sections.title: Reflection shifts some checks to runtime
paragraphs: A direct call such as service.greet() is checked by the compiler against a known type. Looking up getMethod("greet") depends on a string and can fail at runtime if the name or parameter signature is wrong. Method.invoke may also wrap an exception thrown by the invoked method.

The cost and optimizations of reflection depend on the operation and runtime. Do not assume one fixed slowdown factor. Prefer a normal interface for routine application behavior; use reflection where runtime discovery is the purpose. Access checks and module boundaries still apply.

sections.title: A functional interface gives behavior a type
paragraphs: A functional interface has one abstract operation after inherited method rules are taken into account. Default and static methods do not add abstract operations; public methods matching Object methods do not create an extra functional obligation. @FunctionalInterface asks the compiler to verify the contract.

A lambda supplies the implementation of that operation. Its target interface determines parameter types and result type. It is not a free-standing unnamed method that can be assigned to any arbitrary type. The first demonstrations use custom interfaces so the syntax can be understood before generic library interfaces.

sections.title: Parameters, capture, and method references
paragraphs: Parameter types may be inferred, parentheses may be omitted for one inferred parameter, and braces may be omitted for one expression. A lambda may capture instance fields and local variables that are final or effectively final. This restriction gives the captured local value stable meaning even after the method returns.
A method reference is a concise lambda when an existing method already has the required shape. Common forms are Class::staticMethod, object::instanceMethod, Class::instanceMethod, and Class::new.
sections.note: Conciseness is useful only while intent remains obvious. Keep a named lambda when its domain meaning matters.

sections.title: Expression body or block body
paragraphs: An expression lambda returns the expression value when its target requires a result: x -> x * 2. A block lambda uses braces; a value-returning block must explicitly return along every normal result path. A void-compatible callback can perform an action without returning a value.

The lambda uses the enclosing this rather than introducing the anonymous class’s separate this. Captured local variables cannot be reassigned after initialization if that would make them no longer effectively final. An object referenced by such a variable may still be mutable; capture does not make the object immutable or thread-safe.

title: Generics & the Collection Landscape
subtitle: Carry type information through reusable code before choosing a container.
goals: Declare generic classes and methods
Explain bounds, invariance and wildcards
Recognize erasure and its restrictions
Distinguish Collection interfaces from implementations

sections.title: Generic classes and methods
paragraphs: A type parameter is a placeholder chosen when the generic type is used. Box<String> and Box<Integer> share one implementation but expose different compile-time APIs. The diamond operator asks the compiler to infer constructor type arguments.
A generic method declares its own type parameter before its return type. Its type parameter is independent of any type parameter declared by the surrounding class.

sections.title: Invariance and bounded type parameters
paragraphs: Even though Integer extends Number, List<Integer> is not a subtype of List<Number>. If it were, a caller could add a Double to a list that promises to contain only Integer values. Generic types are therefore invariant by default.

A bounded parameter such as <T extends Number> restricts acceptable types and makes Number operations available inside the implementation. Multiple bounds are written with one class bound first, followed by interface bounds.

sections.title: Type parameters belong to declarations
paragraphs: A class-level T is available throughout the instance API of Box<T>. A static method cannot refer to that instance type parameter unless it declares an independent parameter of its own. A generic method places <T> before its return type, for example static <T> T echo(T value).

Use descriptive type names when they improve clarity, such as Key and Value. Generic type arguments must be reference types; use Integer rather than int. Autoboxing can convert primitive values at API boundaries, but unboxing a null wrapper throws NullPointerException.

sections.title: Wildcards and PECS
paragraphs: A wildcard describes a family of parameterized types. List<? extends Number> may refer to a list of Integer, Double, or another Number subtype. It is safe to read values as Number, but unsafe to add a specific number. List<? super Integer> accepts Integer values, but values read from it are known only as Object.
The mnemonic PECS means producer extends, consumer super. Use extends when an argument produces T values for the method; use super when the method consumes or inserts T values.

sections.title: Type erasure and restrictions
paragraphs: Java implements most generics through type erasure. Type arguments guide compilation but are usually not reified as distinct runtime classes. Consequently, code cannot directly create new T(), new T[], test instanceof List<String>, or use primitives such as List<int>.
Raw types such as List bypass generic checking for compatibility with older Java code. They should not be used in new code because they move errors from compilation to runtime.

sections.title: Generic inheritance preserves its declared type
paragraphs: A generic class or interface can be extended or implemented just like a non-generic type. ArrayList<E> implements List<E>, and List<E> extends Collection<E>; the same E is carried through the relationship. A specialized subclass may either keep a parameter open or fix it to one concrete type.

This does not make Box<Integer> a subtype of Box<Number>. Those are two parameterizations of the same generic class and remain invariant. When an API needs a family of related parameterizations, bounded wildcards express that relationship.

sections.title: Erasure does not mean all type information disappears
paragraphs: A type parameter generally erases to Object or its leftmost bound. The compiler inserts casts where necessary and may generate bridge methods so overriding continues to work after erasure. Different parameterizations such as Box<String> and Box<Integer> ordinarily share one runtime class.

Generic signatures may still be recorded as metadata and inspected through reflection. Erasure means that an individual object does not generally carry a reified list element type that can enforce instanceof List<String>. Two overloads whose signatures become identical after erasure are illegal. A static field belongs to the erased class, not separately to each type argument.

sections.title: Collections organize groups of values
paragraphs: A collection framework separates contracts from storage strategies. List promises sequence and positional access; Set promises no duplicates under its equality rule; Queue describes processing order. Map associates keys with values and is part of the framework, but does not extend Collection.

Declare a variable using the smallest interface that expresses the operations needed. List<String> names the contract while new ArrayList<>() selects storage. Generics preserve the element type through add, get and iteration, reducing casts and catching mismatched values at compilation.

sections.title: Choose by required behavior before performance
paragraphs: Ask whether duplicates are allowed, whether positions matter, whether keys identify values, and whether processing order is required. Then choose an implementation. A linked structure is not automatically faster merely because insertion is mentioned: locating an insertion point also costs time.

The next lessons study operations and implementation trade-offs in detail. For now, read List<E> extends Collection<E> extends Iterable<E> as a type relationship that carries the same element parameter forward. This is interface inheritance, separate from invariance between List<Integer> and List<Number>.

title: Lists, Iterators & Queues
subtitle: Manipulate ordered data and make traversal rules explicit.
goals: Use Collection and List operations
Choose ArrayList or LinkedList deliberately
Traverse and remove through an Iterator
Distinguish FIFO queues, deques and priority queues

sections.title: Collection defines common operations
paragraphs: Collection<E> defines operations such as add, remove, contains, size, isEmpty and clear. Bulk operations include addAll, removeAll and retainAll. These are contracts: some implementations do not support every mutation, and optional operations may throw UnsupportedOperationException.

contains and remove(Object) use equality rather than reference identity. List adds positional access, permits duplicate values and defines equality in terms of the same elements in the same order. Set is a different contract and does not gain indexed get simply because it is a collection.

sections.title: ArrayList is a resizable array
paragraphs: ArrayList stores references in an internal array and resizes that storage as needed. get(index) gives constant-time indexed access. Appending is amortized constant time, while inserting or removing near the beginning requires shifting later elements. Size is the number of stored elements; capacity is an internal storage allocation.

remove(1) on a List<Integer> removes the element at index 1. remove(Integer.valueOf(1)) removes the first equal value. This is an important overload distinction. Index bounds run from zero through size - 1 for reading existing elements.

sections.title: LinkedList trades indexing for links
paragraphs: LinkedList stores elements in linked nodes and also implements Deque. Indexed get must traverse nodes, so repeated get(i) inside a large loop can perform much more work than expected. Use an iterator or enhanced for loop for sequential traversal.

Insertion through a positioned list iterator and operations at the ends can update links efficiently. Finding a value or index still takes time. The choice between ArrayList and LinkedList must include access patterns and memory overhead, not just the word “insertion”.

sections.title: Iteration and safe modification
paragraphs: The enhanced for statement is built on Iterable and Iterator. An iterator supplies hasNext(), next(), and sometimes remove(). It separates traversal from the internal representation of the collection.

Structurally modifying most collections while an enhanced-for loop or another iterator is active causes ConcurrentModificationException. Use Iterator.remove(), removeIf(), or collect the desired result into another collection.

sections.title: Implementing Iterable and Iterator
paragraphs: Iterable<T> belongs to the container. Its iterator() method creates an Iterator<T> that owns one traversal cursor. The iterator answers whether an element remains and returns the next element. Returning a fresh iterator allows two loops to traverse the same container independently.

A custom iterator should throw NoSuchElementException when next() is called after exhaustion. The enhanced for statement obtains an iterator automatically, which is why implementing Iterable makes a custom type usable in for-each.

sections.title: Iterable produces iterators; an iterator tracks progress
paragraphs: Iterable<E> supplies iterator(), which returns a cursor over elements. Iterator<E> supplies hasNext() and next(), and may support remove(). An enhanced for loop over an Iterable is syntactic convenience for obtaining and using such an iterator. Arrays are also supported by enhanced for through a separate language translation.

A fresh iterator should represent an independent traversal. next() must throw NoSuchElementException when exhausted, not return an arbitrary null sentinel. Iterator.remove(), when supported, removes the last element returned by next(); it cannot be called twice without another next().

sections.title: Queue and Deque describe processing order
paragraphs: Queue offers add/remove/element methods that can throw on failure and offer/poll/peek alternatives that signal ordinary failure with a special return value. poll and peek return null for an empty queue, which is one reason implementations such as ArrayDeque forbid null elements.

Deque supports both ends. addLast and removeFirst implement a FIFO queue; push and pop use the front for a LIFO stack. ArrayDeque is a useful general starting point for stack or queue behavior when null elements and concurrent access are not required.

sections.title: A PriorityQueue is not a sorted list
paragraphs: PriorityQueue chooses its head by priority, using natural order or an explicit comparator. poll repeatedly removes the smallest remaining element under that ordering. Ties need not preserve insertion order. Iterating or printing the queue does not promise sorted order.

Queue priority does not mean operating-system thread priority. One is an ordering rule for stored elements, the other is a scheduling hint. Keep the concepts separate. For sorted output from a priority queue, deliberately poll until it is empty or copy its elements and sort the copy.

title: Sets, Maps & Natural Ordering
subtitle: Define identity, choose an order, and index data by a stable key.
goals: Keep equals and hashCode consistent
Compare HashSet, LinkedHashSet and TreeSet
Implement Comparable correctly
Choose a Map contract and traverse its entries

sections.title: Hashing narrows the search; equality confirms it
paragraphs: A hash-based collection uses hashCode() to choose a candidate region, then equals() to determine whether the key or element matches. A collision occurs when different objects share a hash value; collisions are legal. Equal objects must have equal hash codes, but equal hash codes do not prove equality.

For a custom Student, decide what defines identity. If ID defines equality, both equals() and hashCode() must use that rule. Do not mutate equality-relevant fields while an object is stored in a hash set or used as a map key. The bucket selected during insertion may no longer match the new hash.

sections.title: Three Set implementations, three ordering promises
paragraphs: HashSet rejects duplicates using equality and offers no iteration-order guarantee. LinkedHashSet also uses equality but preserves insertion order. TreeSet uses comparison to maintain order, and regards elements that compare as zero as equivalent for set membership.

A TreeSet of students ordered only by score may retain just one of two different students sharing that score. Add a tie-breaker when those students must both be stored. Keep natural ordering consistent with equals where possible so the sorted set also satisfies ordinary Set expectations.

sections.title: Comparable defines the type’s natural order
paragraphs: Comparable<T> declares compareTo(T other). Return a negative value when this comes before other, zero when they are equivalent in ordering, and a positive value when this comes after other. The magnitude is unimportant. The ordering must be transitive and its sign must reverse when arguments are swapped.

Use Integer.compare or an appropriate comparison method instead of subtracting integers, because subtraction can overflow. A natural order belongs to the type. Alternate caller-selected orders will be expressed with Comparator in the next lesson.

sections.title: Map contracts and traversal
paragraphs: Map associates unique keys with values but does not extend Collection. HashMap provides no iteration-order guarantee. TreeMap sorts keys. LinkedHashMap preserves insertion order by default.
When both key and value are required, traverse entrySet() so each association is represented directly.

sections.title: Insertion order, access order, and bounded caches
paragraphs: LinkedHashMap's three-argument constructor can enable access order, where successful access moves an entry toward the end. Combining access order with removeEldestEntry supports a bounded least-recently-used policy.
Without accessOrder=true, the same removal hook evicts according to insertion order instead. The constructor choice is therefore part of the data structure's behavior.
sections.note: Do not infer an ordering contract from one printed HashMap result; only documented contracts are portable.

sections.title: Map keys are unique; values need not be
paragraphs: put(key, value) inserts an association or replaces the value for an equal key. get(key) returns the associated value or null if none is mapped; in maps permitting null values, containsKey distinguishes absence from a present null mapping. remove(key) deletes the association.

keySet(), values() and entrySet() are backed views, not independent snapshots. Removing through a supported view removes the corresponding mapping. Traverse entrySet when both key and value are needed. A Map is not directly Iterable, but its views are collections that can be traversed.

sections.title: Choose lookup and order independently
paragraphs: HashMap provides no iteration-order guarantee. LinkedHashMap preserves insertion order by default and can optionally maintain access order. TreeMap stores keys in comparison order and supports sorted-range operations. Null handling differs between implementations; do not assume that all Map implementations accept a null key.

Expected constant-time hash lookup assumes a suitable hash distribution. TreeMap operations such as get and put are logarithmic in entry count. These performance models help choose a starting point; actual workload and memory behavior still matter.

sections.title: An access-ordered map can express a bounded cache
paragraphs: In access-order mode, successful access operations update encounter order. Overriding removeEldestEntry can evict the eldest entry when insertion grows the map beyond a limit. With insertion order instead, the policy evicts the oldest insertion rather than the least recently accessed entry.

This is a small local cache demonstration, not a complete concurrent cache design. Ordinary LinkedHashMap operations are not automatically thread-safe. Keep the cache’s ordering policy separate from the equality rule used to find keys.

title: Sorting, Functional Interfaces & Streams
subtitle: Express a data transformation as a clear sequence with an explicit result.
goals: Compose natural and alternate sorting rules
Use four standard functional interfaces
Build and explain a lazy stream pipeline
Choose terminal operations and avoid shared side effects

sections.title: Specialized and legacy utilities
paragraphs: Properties stores String keys and values and supports configuration load/store formats. BitSet represents non-negative indexes as compact bits and supplies logical set operations.

Hashtable and Enumeration are legacy APIs. StringTokenizer is also a legacy tokenizer. Existing programs may require them, but new designs normally choose HashMap or ConcurrentHashMap, collection views or Iterator, and split, Scanner, or a deliberate parser according to the problem.
sections.note: Recognizing a legacy API does not make it invalid; it means compatibility rather than modern design is usually the reason to retain it.

sections.title: Arrays and Collections are utility classes
paragraphs: Arrays contains static helpers for arrays, including sorting, searching, copying and comparison. Collections contains static algorithms and wrappers for collection objects. Collection is the element-container interface; Collections is a different plural-named utility class.

Arrays.sort changes an array in place. Collections.sort(list) and list.sort(comparator) change a mutable list in place. Binary search requires data sorted under the same ordering used by the search. Arrays.asList returns a fixed-size list backed by its array; new ArrayList<>(...) creates a resizable copy.

sections.title: Comparator supplies an external ordering strategy
paragraphs: Comparator<T> declares compare(left, right), allowing a caller to choose an order without changing the element class. Comparator.comparingInt and comparing extract a sort key; reversed reverses an order and thenComparing resolves ties. Comparable defines one natural order; Comparator can express many alternatives.

Apply reversed at the intended level. comparingInt(score).reversed().thenComparing(name) sorts by descending score and ascending name. Reversing the entire composed comparator would reverse both rules. A tie-breaker makes output deterministic when primary values match.

sections.title: Functional interfaces give lambdas a type
paragraphs: A lambda is not an untyped block of code. Its target type must be a functional interface with exactly one abstract method. The interface determines the parameter types, return type, and allowed checked exceptions. Default and static interface methods do not count against the single-abstract-method rule.

sections.title: Four interfaces represent four common shapes
paragraphs: Predicate<T> takes T and returns boolean through test. Consumer<T> accepts T and performs an action through accept, returning no value. Function<T,R> transforms T to R through apply. Supplier<T> takes no argument and produces T through get. These shapes describe the contract independently of a lambda’s variable names.

Predicates combine with and, or and negate. Functions compose with andThen or compose, whose execution orders differ. A Supplier can delay an expensive fallback until it is required. Creating a lambda usually does not perform the action; calling its interface method does.

sections.title: A stream is a pipeline, not a container
paragraphs: A stream does not store elements. It connects a source to zero or more intermediate operations and one terminal operation. filter, map, distinct, and sorted are intermediate; collect, reduce, count, forEach, and findFirst are terminal.

Intermediate operations are lazy. They perform no traversal until a terminal operation requests a result. This allows the implementation to combine operations and stop early for short-circuiting terminals.

sections.title: Intermediate operations describe a new stream
paragraphs: filter keeps elements matching a predicate. map transforms each element. flatMap flattens a stream of streams. distinct removes duplicates according to equality; sorted orders elements; limit bounds the result. These operations return streams rather than immediately producing a final container.

A pipeline usually pulls each element through the necessary operations instead of completing a full separate traversal for every stage. Stateful operations such as sorted may need to buffer data. A terminal operation can short-circuit: anyMatch may stop at the first match, but sorting before it can still require consuming all input.

sections.title: Choose the terminal result deliberately
paragraphs: count produces a number; anyMatch and allMatch produce booleans; findFirst produces an Optional because no result may exist. collect accumulates results, and reduce combines values with an operation such as addition. For numeric data, mapToInt followed by sum or average avoids repeatedly boxing primitive values.

Stream.toList() produces an unmodifiable list in the Java 21 examples. If later mutation is required, collect with Collectors.toCollection(ArrayList::new). Do not assume Collectors.toList() guarantees a specific mutable implementation. Optional.orElseGet uses a Supplier only when the result is absent.

sections.title: Purity, reuse, and parallelism
paragraphs: A stream is single-use; after a terminal operation, create a new stream for another traversal. Intermediate operations should avoid shared side effects because they make reasoning difficult and may break under parallel execution.

parallelStream() is not an automatic speed switch. Parallel work has coordination costs and requires associative operations, sufficient data, suitable tasks, and measurement. Begin with a correct sequential pipeline and optimize only from evidence.

sections.title: Performance follows the work, not the syntax
paragraphs: A sequential stream can be clear without being faster than a loop. Parallel pipelines need enough independent work to outweigh splitting and coordination. Reduction operations must be associative and have suitable identity values. Side effects on an ordinary shared ArrayList are unsafe in a parallel forEach.

Prefer a collector that manages the reduction rather than external mutation. Encounter order and execution order are different: parallel forEach does not promise encounter-order output, while forEachOrdered preserves it where defined. Measure a representative workload before choosing parallel execution.

sections.title: Build a report from explicit stages
paragraphs: Start with typed records in a list, filter the records that belong in the report, sort with a visible comparator, map each record to the requested representation, and collect the result. Each stage should answer one question that can be stated in a sentence.

Keep storage, validation and presentation separate. A stream reads from the collection; it does not automatically validate domain rules or persist records. The final demonstration uses ordinary classes, a Map index and Stream reporting to connect the concepts from previous lessons without adding a new framework.
